title: 10 Operator Investors to Study Before You Raise an Angel Round
summary: 10 Operator Investors to Study Before You Raise an Angel Round
body_markdown:
When a founder says they want an angel who can help, I want to know what “help” means. If it means intros, to whom? If it's help with hiring, which hire? A founder trying to sell to insurance companies needs someone different from a founder trying to make a mobile app people open every morning.


Work out what you'll need after the money comes in. Most founders can name one problem that will occupy the next six months. That's enough to start: look for someone who's seen it close up and still has a reason to return your call.


## Ten operator investors, with evidence you can check


This is a set of examples, not a ranking or a list of people taking meetings. Some have made personal angel investments; others use funds and syndicates. We separated those routes because they change what it makes sense to ask for.


- [Lenny Rachitsky](https://lennyrachitsky.com/investing) . States interests in AI, B2B software, marketplaces, and consumer products. Research angle: Product adoption and growth.
- [Gokul Rajaram](https://www.gokulrajaram.com/) . Own site lists early investments including Airtable, Faire, and Postman. Research angle: Product strategy and distribution.
- [Elad Gil](https://eladgil.com/) . Own site identifies Gil&Co. and lists past investments. Research angle: Hiring and scaling a technical company.
- [Naval Ravikant](https://www.perplexity.ai/es/hub/blog/perplexity-raises-series-b-funding-round) . Perplexity named him in its Series B announcement. Research angle: Consumer and network-oriented distribution.
- [Cathy Polinsky](https://www.operatorcollective.com/blog-posts/meet-datagrail-cto-cathy-polinsky) . Operator Collective identifies her first angel investment in DataGrail. Research angle: Technical leadership and enterprise adoption.
- [Mallun Yen](https://www.operatorcollective.com/blog-posts/meet-datagrail-cto-cathy-polinsky) . Operator Collective identifies her as an early investor in DataGrail. Research angle: Enterprise and operator introductions.
- [Sahil Lavingia](https://www.angellist.com/blog/easier-than-expected-gumroad-ceo-on-launching-his-first) . AngelList documents the Gumroad founder’s launch of a rolling fund. Research angle: Creator tools and monetization.
- [Julian Shapiro](https://www.julian.com/guide/angel/intro) . Own writing identifies Julian Capital and Deep Checks as investing vehicles. Research angle: Early marketing and technical-market research.
- [Ryan Hoover](https://usvc.com/announcement/investing-in-weekend-fund-iv) . USVC discloses its investment in Weekend Fund IV and describes the team. Research angle: Product launches and distribution.
- [Jason Calacanis](https://thesyndicate.com/) . The Syndicate identifies him as its lead and lists its relationship to LAUNCH. Research angle: Syndicate participation rather than assuming a personal check.


## Think about the job you need the angel to do


Ask founders you've worked with who gave them useful advice before they were obviously succeeding. Then ask what the advice changed. The person who helped set up their first pricing experiment is a stronger recommendation than the person whose name went on the investor slide.


Take a first call with a concrete question. For example: “Hospitals love the pilot but nobody owns the rollout budget. At your last company, who needed to sign off before a pilot became a contract?” An answer you can test next week tells you more about working together than an hour of agreement about the size of the market.


Keep the buying process straight. A personal check, a syndicate, and a fund approval don't happen the same way. Confirm who's making the decision and which entity will sign. Record it with the stage, the public evidence, and a follow-up date. Until then, don't turn “I'd love to help” into an amount in your cash forecast.
